prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, reaching unprecedented accuracy and stability in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: After reading the opening ballots I move my preferred configuration from B005 to B015. Optical lattice clocks rest on a clear, original idea (the magic-wavelength lattice, which removes the light shift while keeping Lamb-Dicke confinement and many-atom averaging) and on a decisive demonstration that took fractional uncertainty to about 1e-18. The result has been reproduced by many independent laboratories and compared across continents, so maturity is not in doubt. It also matters beyond metrology: tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and the roadmap for redefining the second. It is the only shortlisted candidate that all eight members ranked, and the two credited names (Katori for the concept and first strontium clock, Ye for taking the performance to the frontier) are the one allocation nobody has contested. I still regard B005 as the strongest fundamental-theory case on the list, and I keep it as my first alternative, but I cannot claim a statistical-physics preference is a better basis for a prize than a result the whole committee can defend.
statement.case_against: The main reservation is domain overlap. Frequency combs and precision spectroscopy were honoured in 2005 and the control of single trapped ions in 2012, so a clock prize may look like a third helping from the same area, and the strongest practical payoff, a redefined second, has not happened yet. There is also a risk that the broad consensus reflects familiarity rather than an independent judgement of discovery value: a field-neutral reader could ask whether this is an exceptional advance in physics or an exceptional improvement of an instrument. Finally, ion-clock groups and lattice-clock co-developers who are not in the credited names (Ludlow, Lemke and others in Ye's group, for example) are left out by a two-name credit.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B015 first because the magic-wavelength concept plus the Ye-group demonstrations give a clean, mature, timely prize, with the credited pair covering the core of the work.
responses.response: I agree on the science and on the pair. Where I would qualify is her suggestion that the redefinition of the second makes the timing obviously right. The prize does not depend on that milestone, and I would not want the citation to lean on an application that is still pending. I would phrase it around the invention and the achieved accuracy, and I accept her point that Ye's contribution is the quantitative realisation, not only the performance record.

responses.point: Olsson places topological insulators (B018) first as a new class of matter in which theory and experiment fit together, with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan as the decisive chain, and notes that Mele and the HgTe proposers are awkward omissions.
responses.response: I ranked B018 second and agree that it is arguably an overdue omission. My difficulty is the same one she names: any three-person selection leaves out Mele, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and Hasan's three-dimensional work sits beside, not inside, the Kane-Molenkamp quantum spin Hall chain. B003 and B018 also compete for the same ground, so the committee would have to settle that internally first. B015 has no such attribution problem, which is why I now put it ahead, but I keep B018 as an alternative and would support it if the committee can agree on a credit line.

responses.point: Danielsson (supported by Pearce) puts IceCube's high-energy astrophysical neutrinos (B014) first, as a clear nameable discovery of nature that opened a new messenger, with Halzen and Karle as a compact credit.
responses.response: I agree it is a discovery of nature and the experimental achievement is remarkable. I ranked it fifth for two reasons. The diffuse flux is well confirmed, but the source interpretation is still unsettled, so part of the claim is not yet mature. And a very large collaboration with AMANDA and DUMAND antecedents is being represented by two names, which leaves a real attribution question that I cannot settle from the supplied record. I would not oppose it, but I do not think it is more secure than the clocks.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B015 first and B032 (optical-lattice quantum simulation) third, placing both in the line of precision atomic physics and ultracold-atom control, and judges the credit compact and fair.
responses.response: I share his view on B015. On B032 I am less settled: the Mott-transition experiments and the broader quantum-simulation programme are different things, and the allocation among Zoller, Bloch, Greiner and Cirac is awkward when the same names appear in the trapped-ion candidate B009. I would not add B032 to my alternatives for that reason, and I would argue that awarding B015 does not preempt an ultracold-atom prize later.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the 2005 and 2012 prizes as having already covered enough of precision atomic physics to make a lattice-clock prize less urgent.
Whether to credit only Katori and Ye or whether the committee thinks other lattice-clock developers deserve consideration; the supplied record does not resolve this.
Whether B005 can attract any support beyond mine, given that attribution among Evans, Gallavotti-Cohen, Jarzynski and Crooks is contested and I am relying on my own recollection of the history.
Whether the topological-insulator candidates (B018, B003) can reach an agreed three-name credit that colleagues accept.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. B005 and B032 touch statistical physics, which is my field, but I have no documented connection to the credited candidates, and I note that my opening first-place ranking for B005 reflects subject-matter preference only.
